To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cancer cells respond to a variety of compounds in a manner which is different from that of normal cells.

the in vitro synthesis and strand separation of cancer DNA are much more stimulated than normal DNA by the above-mentioned chemicals and that the accelerated multiplication of cancer cells in vivo in the presence of these substances correlates with their effect on cancer DNA in vitro.
cancer DNA is more sensitive to DNA strand separation than is DNA from normal tissues, and that DNA synthesis is stimulated in vitro and in vivo by the compounds studied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the search for new anticancer agents, with the elucidation of the mechanisms of cancer development and of the mechanisms of action of anticancer agents.
the search for new drugs which are able to distinguish cancer DNA and cancer cells from normal DNA and healthy cells.
the study of cancer cell DNA and the search for compounds which could be useful as anticancer drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DNA strand separation is an important step in the process of DNA synthesis and that this separation is a function of cancer cells and not a function of normal cells.

the in vitro synthesis and strand separation of cancer DNA are stimulated by all compounds tested, whereas the synthesis and strand separation in normal DNA is stimulated only by croton oil and by DMSO.
the in vitro synthesis and the in vivo multiplication of Ehrich cancer cells are correlated with the degree of strand separation of the DNA of these cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cancer cells are more susceptible to the action of carcinogens, carcinogenic chemicals, mutagens, antineoplastic drugs and other substances which are not necessarily toxic to normal cells.
DNA synthesis, DNA separation, and cell multiplication are all interdependent and that these three parameters are more sensitive to cancer cells than to normal cells.
the DNA synthesis and strand separation in vitro are not only stimulated but also differentiated by the compounds tested.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNA synthesis, DNA hyperchromicity and cell proliferation are closely correlated in cancer cells, but not in normal cells.

the compounds tested stimulate the synthesis of DNA in vitro and in vivo and that this effect may be due to an increase in the number of double-stranded DNA regions in the presence of these compounds.
DNA strand separation, which is a characteristic property of cancer cells, can be used to detect the presence of cancer DNA in the presence of DNA from healthy cells.
